title: Chi Kung: eight standing postures for beginners
excerpt: A step-by-step guide to the eight standing Chi Kung postures practised in EmptyHands Tai Chi classes, with the key pressure points and what each posture offers for health and for martial practice.
html:
Chi Kung (气功, also written Qigong) means “energy work”. It is the quiet side of Tai Chi Chuan: posture, breathing and attention, practised standing still. In EmptyHands Tai Chi classes, students work through a short set of eight standing postures that settle the breath, align the body and prepare it for the form. The postures are taught in line with the teachings of the Master Ding Academy, where Azeem Sensei has studied traditional Yang family Tai Chi Chuan since 1999 with Master John Ding and Sifu Doosyant Mahadeo.

The postures look simple, and they are. The skill lies in holding them with a relaxed body and a quiet mind, and that is where both the health benefits and the martial value come from. This guide takes you through each posture, what to feel, and the pressure points to be aware of.

Before you start

Every posture shares the same foundations:

  • Feet parallel and pointing straight forward, not turned out, and exactly shoulder-width apart.
  • Weight on the balls of the feet, rooting through Yongquan (KI1), the Bubbling Spring.
  • Head lifted from the crown through Baihui (GV20), with the chin gently tucked in.
  • Chest hollowed and the back raised, so the upper body is rounded rather than puffed out.
  • Shoulders relaxed, with the elbows down.
  • Knees “melted”, slightly bent, in postures 2 to 7, and straight in postures 1 and 8.

The whole set can be summed up in one line: Baihui lifts, Shen Men opens, Lao Gong relaxes, Yong Quan roots. The crown lifts, the wrists soften, the palms relax and the feet root into the ground. Do not focus hard on the points. Let them open naturally through good posture and relaxation.

The eight postures

1. Wu Chi: stillness

Stand upright with the legs straight and let the arms hang by your sides, middle fingers resting on the seams of your trousers. Here they touch Fengshi (GB31) on the outer thigh, while the palms (Lao Gong, PC8) and wrists (Shen Men, HT7) stay soft.

Wu Chi (无极) means “without extremes”: the empty, balanced state before movement begins. Every Tai Chi form starts and finishes here, and alignment you can find in stillness is far easier to keep in motion.

2. Hands to the Mouth: the breath

Melt the knees and raise the hands to mouth level, keeping the shoulders relaxed and the elbows down. Be aware of the thumbs, where the Lung channel ends (Shaoshang, LU11), and the index fingers, where its partner, the Large Intestine channel, begins (Shangyang, LI1).

This posture links the stance with the breath. Raising the hands without lifting the shoulders is also one of the first lessons of Tai Chi: the arms are carried by the body, not hoisted by the shoulders.

3. Holding the Large Ball: sinking the elbows

Drop the arms down as if holding a large beach ball, fingertips dropping downwards. The elbows point outwards but stay relaxed, and the arms are held away from the body. As the elbows sink, the points around them open, especially Quchi (LI11) at the outer end of the elbow crease.

The rounded, springy arms are an early taste of peng (掤), the buoyant, expanding energy Tai Chi uses to absorb and redirect force. Dropping the elbows keeps the arms connected to the body and protects the ribs.

4. Palms Turn Outwards: opening the heart

Bring the arms up with the palms facing outwards, shoulders relaxed and elbows down. Let the little fingers lengthen. The Heart channel runs through the inner elbow and the wrist (Shen Men, HT7, the “Spirit Gate”) to the little finger (Shaochong, HT9).

The Heart channel is linked with a calm mind, and many people feel this posture open the chest and release tension across the shoulders.

5. Palms Press Down: the palm heart

Bring the arms down with the palms facing the ground and the elbows out. Keep the arms away from the body and everything relaxed, including the waist. The elbows sink again, and attention moves to the centre of the palms, Lao Gong (PC8), the “Palace of Labour”.

Lao Gong is often the first place students feel warmth or tingling. A useful reminder for this posture is: open the Lao Gong, soften the Shen Men, sink the elbows, lift Baihui. Martially, it trains sinking: the feeling of weight dropping through the palms, legs and feet into the ground.

6. Holding the Small Ball: listening energy

Bring the arms in front of the chest as if holding a smaller ball, palms pushing slightly outwards. Feel the ball through the palms (Lao Gong, PC8), with the heart centre, Danzhong (CV17), behind it.

This posture is about ting jin (聽勁), listening energy. Ting means to listen, not with the ears but by feeling, and jin is trained, refined power. In push hands, ting jin is the ability to sense a partner’s force, balance and intention through contact, before they become obvious.

7. Resting on the Armchair: arousing the energy

Bring the hands down to hip level, as if resting your forearms straight on the arms of an armchair. The upper arms and elbows relax by the sides, and the forearms and hands are flat, with the fingers pointing forward.

Here the intention extends forward from the palms through the fingertips. In Tai Chi this is described as the mind (yi) leading the energy (qi): “the fingers reach, but do not stretch”. Intent without tension is the same quality that lets a Tai Chi technique be both relaxed and fast.

8. Hands on the Dantian: settling the energy

Stand up slowly and bring the hands together over the lower abdomen, just below the navel. Men place the left hand against the body and cover it with the right; women place the right hand against the body and cover it with the left. This follows the traditional yin-yang correspondence. Half close the eyes and breathe gently.

The palms now rest over the lower dantian, the body’s centre, around Qihai (CV6, the “Sea of Qi”) and Guanyuan (CV4). “Where the mind goes, qi follows”: attention settles, the breath deepens and energy sinks back down. Never skip this closing posture.

Why stand still?

For health and wellbeing, standing practice gently strengthens the legs, improves posture and trains balance, while slow, relaxed breathing calms the nervous system. Research on Tai Chi and Qigong has linked regular practice with better balance and fewer falls in older adults, lower stress, better sleep and improved mood. Many people simply find that ten quiet minutes standing leaves them calmer and more focused for the rest of the day.

For the martial artist, this kind of standing, known as zhan zhuang (站桩, “standing like a post”), has long been treated as the foundation of the internal arts. It builds root through the legs, a structure that stays aligned under pressure, and the relaxation that lets power travel from the feet to the hands. The same principles sit underneath a strong Karate stance.

How to practise

  • Begin with a minute or two in each posture and build up over the weeks. The whole set takes 10 to 20 minutes.
  • Breathe naturally through the nose, without forcing or holding the breath.
  • Move slowly and smoothly from one posture to the next.
  • Practise daily if you can. First thing in the morning works well.
  • Keep the knees soft and over the toes, never locked or pushed past them.
  • Stop if you feel pain or dizziness, and check with your GP first if you have a health condition or injury.

Pressure points at a glance

Learn it in class

Chi Kung is best learned with a teacher who can check your alignment. Tai Chi Chuan classes run every Thursday from 6pm to 7pm at St Andrew’s Church Hall, The Drive, Ilford, and beginners of all ages are welcome. Read more about Tai Chi at EmptyHands and the health benefits of Tai Chi, or book your first class.

title: EmptyHands at 20: two decades of discipline, growth and community
excerpt: In March 2006 a small dojo opened its doors in Ilford. Twenty years, hundreds of students and fifteen black belts later, a look back at the people and moments that made EmptyHands.
html:
Twenty years ago a simple idea took root in East London. It was never about building the biggest martial arts school, producing champions or creating a brand. It was about making a place where people could learn, challenge themselves and discover what martial arts can offer beyond punching and kicking.

In March 2006, Azeem Mushtaq Sensei founded EmptyHands in Ilford on the principles of Bushidō: discipline, respect, humility and purpose. Since then, hundreds of students and their families have trained, grown and found a second home at the dojo. This anniversary is a moment to look back at the people, the challenges and the milestones that made EmptyHands what it is.

Twenty years at a glance

  • 1994 - Azeem begins his formal Karate training as a founding member of an East London dojo.
  • 1999 - He launches ZenKarate, one of the first online Karate magazines, and begins studying Tai Chi Chuan with Master John Ding.
  • 2003 - He graduates from the British School of Shiatsu-Dō and founds the EmptyHands clinic.
  • 2006 - EmptyHands opens its doors in Ilford.
  • 2011 - The dojo awards its first black belt.
  • 2013 - Azeem completes an MA in Coaching at Oxford Brookes, developing the first Karate Coaching Model.
  • 2020 - The Virtual Dojo keeps students training together through lockdown.
  • 2026 - Twenty years, fifteen black belts, and classes in Karate, Tai Chi, Yoga, Shiatsu and Coaching.

The beginning

The roots of EmptyHands go back long before 2006. Inspired by a family tradition of wrestling, Azeem discovered martial arts as a child and took up kickboxing as a teenager at the Gold Steel Gym in Walthamstow. After starting formal Karate training in 1994, he trained widely, learning from respected teachers including Hirokazu Kanazawa Sōke, Chris Rowen Shihan, Yoshinobu Ohta Sensei and Nobuaki Kanazawa Kanchō, while Tai Chi Chuan and Shiatsu broadened his understanding of movement, health and human performance.

By 2006 the vision was clear: one school that would bring martial arts, wellbeing and personal growth together under one roof.

Building a community

Over twenty years, hundreds of students have stepped onto the dojo floor. Some came for self-defence; others wanted fitness, confidence, discipline, friendship or simply a new challenge. Many stayed far longer than they expected. Children grew into adults, beginners became senior grades and students became instructors, among them founding members Hamza Iftikhar and Amarah Adam, who now help teach the next generation. For many, the dojo became a second family.

The path to black belt

Among the school’s proudest achievements are the fifteen students who have earned their black belt since the first was awarded in December 2011, some of whom started training at the age of three. A black belt is not an award for perfection. It stands for commitment, resilience, patience and a willingness to keep learning long after others have stopped. Each of them is celebrated on the Yudansha wall, and each is proof that success is rarely about talent alone. It is about showing up, week after week, year after year.

A school that kept evolving

Karate remains at the heart of EmptyHands, but Tai Chi Chuan, Yoga, Shiatsu and Coaching have become part of the school too. They reflect a simple belief: martial arts are not just about fighting, they are about living well. Balance, awareness, recovery and emotional resilience all belong on the path.

Learning from great teachers

Every martial artist stands on the shoulders of those who came before. Workshops with Chris Rowen Shihan gave karateka of every grade the chance to train with a world authority on Goju-Ryu Karate, who trained in Japan under Gogen Yamaguchi, and the school’s wider network has connected students with leading practitioners of Karate, Tai Chi and Shiatsu.

One relationship deserves special mention. Azeem first met the renowned Shiatsu master Rex Lassalle in 2010, and what began as treatment grew into a lasting friendship. Rex shaped Azeem’s understanding of Shiatsu and in 2024 taught his Be Easy Sōtai method at the dojo. He died in February 2025, and his teaching, generosity and friendship remain an important chapter in the EmptyHands story. Read the tribute to Rex.

Giving back

The spirit of EmptyHands has always reached beyond the dojo walls, through demonstrations, workshops, charity activities and local events. The annual EmptyHands Charity Cup has become one of the school’s most cherished traditions. Open to every grade, it combines kata, kumite and team events with fundraising for a chosen charity each year.

A test like no other

Perhaps the greatest test came in 2020, when the COVID-19 pandemic closed training halls. Rather than pause, the school moved online. Through the Virtual Dojo on Microsoft Teams, students kept training, supported one another and held on to routines that had become an important part of their lives. Apart physically, the community stayed connected.

The people behind the school

No anniversary would be complete without thanking the instructors, assistants, parents, families and volunteers who helped shape EmptyHands.

Special recognition goes to Irm Mushtaq Sensei, who began training in 2006, the year the dojo opened, and is now a SanDan (third-degree black belt) and Senior Instructor. Through years of coaching, mentoring and running the dojo day to day, and as the founder of EmptyHands Yoga, she has helped countless students begin and continue their journeys. Generations of senior students have also stepped forward to lead warm-ups, guide beginners and mentor younger members. Their work often goes unnoticed, but it is the foundation the school stands on.

Lessons from twenty years

The most remarkable achievements of EmptyHands cannot be measured in belts or grades. They can be seen in the shy child who found confidence, the student who overcame anxiety, the adult who found resilience after difficult times, and the families and friendships the dojo brought together.

Looking back on two decades, Azeem Sensei reflects:

“Twenty years of running EmptyHands has taught me that a dojo is never really about the instructor, the style or even the building. It is about the students, and helping them discover what they are capable of becoming. There have been successes and setbacks, lasting friendships and, inevitably, some people lost along the way. It is impossible to please everyone, but it is always possible to act with sincerity and purpose.

The greatest lesson of all has been humility. Through teaching the principles of Bushidō, I have come to understand that true martial arts are not measured by skill alone, but by character. Integrity, respect, compassion and good conduct remain the highest achievements. In the end, belts fade and trophies gather dust, but the values we pass on to others endure. That is the true legacy of a dojo.”

Looking forward

EmptyHands enters its third decade with gratitude to everyone who has been part of the journey, and with the same aim it began with. As the first line of the Dojo Kun puts it: seek perfection of character. Whether you trained for a few weeks, a few years or the whole twenty, thank you. You are part of the EmptyHands story.

If you trained at EmptyHands at any point, we would love to hear from you: get in touch and share your memories. And if you have never stepped onto the dojo floor, there is no better time to begin. Book a trial class and start your own chapter.

Here’s to the next twenty years. Osu.

title: In memory of Rex Lassalle (1945-2025)
excerpt: Remembering Rex Lassalle, Shiatsu pioneer, founder of the Hara Shiatsu School, and teacher and friend of EmptyHands, who died on 13 February 2025.
html:
It is with great sadness that we remember the passing of Rex Lassalle, who died on 13 February 2025 at the age of 79. Yet while his passing marked the end of an extraordinary life, his influence continues to live on through the thousands of practitioners, students and patients whose lives he touched.

To many, Rex was a master of Shiatsu. To those who knew him personally, he was much more: a teacher, healer, pioneer, philosopher, mentor and friend.

A pioneer of Shiatsu

Over a lifetime dedicated to understanding health and human potential, Rex became one of the most influential figures in the development of Shiatsu in the United Kingdom. After training in osteopathy and immersing himself in Eastern healing traditions, he went on to found the Hara Shiatsu School in London in 1986 and helped establish Shiatsu as a respected therapeutic discipline throughout Britain and Europe. His work combined traditional Japanese healing arts with an exceptional understanding of movement, bodywork, Five Element theory and East Asian philosophy.

Rex never stopped exploring. Whether through Shiatsu, osteopathy, Aikido, Sōtai, Oriental medicine or his extensive writings on Nine Star Ki and the nature of time, he was driven by a desire to help people better understand themselves and live healthier, more balanced lives. His teaching was profound yet practical. He had a unique gift for making complex ideas accessible and meaningful.

Rex and EmptyHands

At EmptyHands, Rex’s legacy carries a special significance.

Azeem Mushtaq first met Rex in 2010 when seeking Shiatsu treatment. What began as a therapeutic relationship soon grew into a lasting friendship. Over the following years they worked closely on numerous initiatives, workshops and educational projects, united by a shared commitment to wellbeing and personal development.

Azeem often reflected that some of the greatest lessons he received from Rex had little to do with technique. Rex taught through example. He demonstrated the importance of curiosity, humility, lifelong learning and genuine care for others. His wisdom helped shape Azeem’s understanding of Shiatsu and continues to influence the philosophy and practice of EmptyHands today.

In 2024, we had the privilege of welcoming Rex to our dojo to teach his “Be Easy Sōtai” method. Watching him work was a reminder that true mastery is often expressed through simplicity. Decades of experience had distilled into a gentle, accessible approach that empowered people to reconnect with their bodies and discover health through ease rather than force.

A lasting legacy

What made Rex exceptional was not merely his knowledge, but his willingness to share it. He inspired generations of practitioners to think differently about health, healing and personal responsibility. His influence can be found throughout the modern Shiatsu community in the UK, where many of the approaches and perspectives now considered commonplace bear the imprint of his pioneering work.

Today, as we look back on his life, we give thanks for the immense contribution he made to the healing arts. We remember a man who dedicated himself to helping others, who challenged convention, who remained a student throughout his life, and who generously shared his wisdom with all who crossed his path.

Rex Lassalle leaves behind a remarkable legacy. His teachings continue through his books, his students, his schools and the countless practitioners he inspired. Most importantly, they continue in the lives of those who have been helped by the healing traditions he championed.

Thank you, Rex, for your guidance, friendship and vision. Your hands may be still, but your work lives on.

“A teacher’s greatest legacy is not what they leave behind, but what they awaken in others.”

title: The health benefits of Tai Chi
excerpt: Tai Chi Chuan develops health, wellbeing and practical self-defence in a single practice: calm, focus, balance and confidence for students and for people of every age.
html:
Students today face a unique challenge. Academic pressures are increasing, screen time is higher than ever, and opportunities for genuine physical, mental, and emotional balance can be difficult to find. Tai Chi Chuan offers a remarkable solution because it develops health, wellbeing, and practical self-defence skills within a single practice.

Originally created as a sophisticated Chinese martial art, Tai Chi goes far beyond the slow movements that many people associate with it. At its heart, it is a complete training system that develops strength, balance, coordination, focus, and resilience. The gentle, flowing exercises improve posture, flexibility, and body awareness while placing minimal stress on the joints. This makes it suitable for people of all ages and fitness levels.

Calm and focus

For students, the wellbeing benefits are particularly valuable. Regular practice encourages calmness, improves concentration, and helps reduce the effects of stress and anxiety. The combination of mindful movement and controlled breathing trains the mind to become more focused and less reactive. Many students find that the same skills that help them remain balanced during practice also help them stay composed during exams, presentations, and everyday challenges.

Strength, balance and posture

The physical benefits are equally impressive. Tai Chi develops functional strength, stability, and coordination throughout the entire body. Unlike many forms of exercise that focus solely on external fitness, Tai Chi teaches efficient movement, correct alignment, and relaxation under pressure. These skills can improve performance in sports, reduce the likelihood of injuries, and support lifelong health.

A genuine martial art

Perhaps most interestingly, Tai Chi remains a genuine martial art. Beneath the graceful movements lies a system designed to cultivate timing, sensitivity, balance, structure, and self-defence ability. Students learn how to remain relaxed and composed in challenging situations rather than relying on force alone. The principles developed through partner work and martial applications build confidence, self-control, and discipline, qualities that are valuable both inside and outside the training hall.

In a world that often encourages speed, distraction, and constant activity, Tai Chi teaches something increasingly rare: how to be calm, centred, and effective at the same time. It develops a healthy body, a focused mind, and a confident spirit.

Getting started

You do not need previous experience, athletic ability, or exceptional fitness to begin. Simply attending a beginner’s class can open the door to a practice that has benefited people for centuries. Whether your goal is better health, greater wellbeing, improved concentration, self-defence skills, or personal growth, Tai Chi Chuan offers a path worth exploring.

Sometimes the strongest person is not the fastest or the most forceful, but the one who has learned to remain balanced, focused, and at ease whatever life brings. Tai Chi Chuan teaches exactly that.

title: Benefits of Shotokan Karate
excerpt: Shotokan Karate builds far more than strong kicks and punches. Through the five Dojo Kun it shapes character, confidence, discipline and respect - on the dojo floor and beyond it.
html:
Ask people why they start Karate and most will say fitness or self-defence. Ask them why they stay, and the answer is usually different: it is the person Karate helps them become. At EmptyHands we follow the classical Shotokan system, and every class ends with the Dojo Kun - five precepts that carry the heart of the art.

The five Dojo Kun

The Dojo Kun were handed down by the masters of Shotokan as a guide for training and for life. Students recite them together at the end of every lesson. Each one begins with hitotsu - “one” - because each is as important as the others.

1. To strive for the perfection of character

一、人格完成に努むること · Hitotsu, jinkaku kansei ni tsutomuru koto

This is the first and most important aim of Karate. Perfection is never reached, but striving towards it - being a little more patient, honest and kind each week - is the real training. Kicks and punches are the tools; character is the goal.

2. To defend the path of truth

一、誠の道を守ること · Hitotsu, makoto no michi o mamoru koto

Be sincere, with others and with yourself. In the dojo that means training honestly: admitting what you can’t do yet, and never pretending a technique is better than it is. Outside the dojo it means standing up for what is right, even when it is difficult.

3. To foster the spirit of effort

一、努力の精神を養うこと · Hitotsu, doryoku no seishin o yashinau koto

Progress in Karate comes from steady, patient effort - the same stance practised a thousand times, the same kata polished year after year. Students learn that hard work, more than talent, carries them from white belt to black belt, and that lesson goes with them into school, exams and work.

4. To honour the principles of etiquette

一、礼儀を重んずること · Hitotsu, reigi o omonzuru koto

Karate begins and ends with a bow. Respect for the Sensei, for training partners and for the dojo itself makes it a safe place to learn. Good manners become a habit, and courtesy is often the first change parents notice in their children.

5. To guard against impetuous courage

一、血気の勇を戒むること · Hitotsu, kekki no yū o imashimuru koto

Real strength includes self-control. Karate teaches students to stay calm, think before they act and walk away from trouble whenever they can. The aim is never to look for a fight, but to have the composure to avoid one.

How Karate builds confidence

Confidence grows in the dojo one small step at a time. A nervous beginner learns a first stance, then a first kata, and one day stands in front of the class at a grading to show what they can do. Every new belt is proof that effort pays off.

Because everyone is taught to respect their training partners, the dojo is a safe place to make mistakes and try again. Shy children start to speak up, look people in the eye and lead the warm-up for younger students. Adults find a calm self-assurance that comes from knowing their body and mind are stronger than they were.

Knowing how to look after yourself brings a quiet confidence too - not a need to prove anything, but the security of knowing you could protect yourself if you ever had to.

How Karate builds discipline

Discipline in Karate is learned, not imposed. Students arrive on time, line up by grade, bow in and listen when the Sensei speaks. Week by week, these small routines become habits.

Kihon teaches patience: the same punch or block repeated until it is right, and then repeated again. Kata asks for concentration from the first movement to the last. Gradings give students a goal and a date to work towards, so they learn to practise between lessons rather than waiting to be told.

Parents often tell us that this self-discipline shows up at home and at school - in homework done without an argument, in better concentration and in a calmer response to setbacks.

How Karate teaches respect

Respect runs through every part of a Karate class. Students bow as they enter and leave the dojo, before and after working with a partner, and to the Sensei at the start and end of every lesson. The bow is a reminder that everyone in the room is there to learn, and that each partner trusts the other with their safety.

Control is respect in action: in kumite, techniques are delivered with full spirit but stopped before they can hurt a partner. Senior students help beginners, and beginners learn from those who once stood where they stand. Children learn to respect adults, and adults learn just as much from the enthusiasm of children.

Respect also turns inwards - looking after your body, keeping your word and living by the Dojo Kun outside the dojo as well as inside it.

More benefits of Shotokan Karate

  • Fitness at any age - strength, flexibility, balance and stamina, built through kihon, kata and partner work at a pace that suits each student.
  • Focus and memory - learning long kata sequences sharpens memory and concentration.
  • Practical self-defence - bunkai (the application of kata) and controlled kumite teach timing, distance and awareness.
  • A calmer mind - breathing, a moment of mokuso (meditation) and the rhythm of training help to ease everyday stress. A 2020 review of research found that martial arts training can improve mental wellbeing too.
  • Friendship and community - children and adults from every background train side by side, and senior students mentor those just starting out.

Start your own journey

Karate classes run every Thursday from 7pm to 9pm at St Andrew’s Church Hall, The Drive, Ilford IG1 3PE, for children from 4 and adults of any age. New starters pay as they go at £10 a lesson, and all you need is comfortable clothes. Book a trial class, or read more about Karate classes in Ilford.

title: Reflections: lessons from lockdown
excerpt: How Karate, Yoga, daily walks, good food and a little gardening helped one EmptyHands teacher stay calm and keep a healthy routine through lockdown.
html:
When the Coronavirus lockdown began, daily life changed almost overnight. This is a short reflection on the practices that helped me keep a routine and stay calm when everything around us felt uncertain.

Time to stop and practise

Lockdown gave me a chance to do something we rarely do: stop. With more time at home, I could practise Karate more often. Learning new kata and refining old ones brought energy, focus and a sense of regularity when it was needed most.

A steady routine of warm-ups, stances and kihon felt like a samurai polishing his sword, removing a little more each day. I added breathing exercises, sometimes with a stick of sandalwood incense burning, which helped me focus on the breath and the task in hand.

Yoga on the mat

Regular Yoga practice was a lifesaver. Working through the postures builds strength, flexibility and balance, and any sense of unease fades as you settle on the mat. As in Karate, linking posture and breath helps energy move freely. I always finished with a feeling of calm as the mat was rolled up and put away.

A daily walk in the forest

A daily walk to the local forest, with a few uphill sprints, built stamina and gave me fresh air and quiet. When movement and contact with others were restricted, combining exercise with time outdoors became essential for both body and mind.

Eating well

Good food is part of training. I aimed for colourful meals with plenty of fruit, vegetables and lentils, eaten in season and organic where possible. With so much attention on health and immunity, a balanced diet felt more important than ever, and trying new foods became a small adventure of its own.

Noticing the world around us

Lockdown also taught me to appreciate my surroundings: the many shades of green in the garden, the shapes and textures of plants, and the radishes, fenugreek and mangetout slowly growing towards harvest. Even watching fish content in a small pond was a reminder to value what we have.

If there is one lesson to take from that time, it is this: use the time you have for whatever part of your training inspires you.

title: The history of Karate-Dō
excerpt: From the legends of Shaolin to the islands of Okinawa and the Shotokan dojo in Tokyo: a short history of how Karate-Dō became a martial art practised worldwide.
html:
Karate-Dō, the “way of the empty hand”, is practised by millions of people around the world. Its story stretches back centuries and across several countries, from China to the islands of Okinawa and on to mainland Japan.

Legends of Shaolin

Many martial arts trace their spiritual roots to the Shaolin Monastery on Mount Song in Henan, China. Tradition says that the Buddhist monk Bodhidharma arrived there from India in the 5th or 6th century AD, meditated for nine years and taught the monks exercises to strengthen body and mind. Historians treat the link between Bodhidharma and fighting arts as legend rather than record, but the idea that martial training is also a path of self-development runs through Karate to this day.

Okinawa: the birthplace of Karate

Karate itself developed on Okinawa, the main island of the Ryukyu Kingdom, which traded closely with China from the late 1300s. Local fighting methods, known simply as te (hand), blended with Chinese boxing brought by envoys, merchants and students. The result became known as tō-de (唐手), “Tang hand” or “Chinese hand”, and was taught quietly in towns such as Shuri, Naha and Tomari.

From Okinawa to Japan

In the early 20th century, Okinawan masters began teaching more openly, including in schools. In 1922 the Okinawan teacher Gichin Funakoshi demonstrated the art in Tokyo and stayed to teach it on the Japanese mainland. In the 1930s the first character of the name was changed to 空, meaning “empty”, so that karate came to mean “empty hand”, and the suffix dō (way) was added to stress the art’s role in developing character.

Funakoshi’s students named his dojo Shōtōkan after his pen name, Shōtō, meaning “pine waves”. The Shotokan tiger became its emblem, and the style spread across Japan and then the world.

Karate today

After the Second World War, Karate spread rapidly through Europe and America. Many styles grew from the Okinawan roots, among them Shotokan, Goju-Ryu, Shito-Ryu and Wado-Ryu, and Karate made its Olympic debut at the Tokyo Games in 2021.

At EmptyHands, students learn traditional Shotokan Karate, with influences from Goju-Ryu, following a syllabus inspired by the late Hirokazu Kanazawa Sōke. Every class still works through the same foundations the masters handed down: kihon, kata, bunkai and kumite. Read more about Karate classes in Ilford.

title: Sports injuries and the martial arts
excerpt: Common martial arts injuries, how to prevent them, what to do when one happens, and how EmptyHands supports students through injury and recovery.
html:
Any physical activity carries some risk of injury, and contact sports and martial arts are no exception. The good news is that most injuries are minor, and many can be prevented with sensible training. This article explains the common types of injury, how to reduce the risk, and what to do if you are hurt.

Types of sports injury

Sports injuries are often grouped into three broad categories:

  • Minor injuries - grazes, blisters, bruises, muscle soreness, cramp and mild sprains.
  • Moderate injuries - pulled or strained muscles, more serious sprains and stress fractures.
  • Major injuries - torn tendons or ligaments, broken bones and concussion.

Preventing injury in the dojo

  • Warm up properly. A good warm-up raises the heart rate and prepares joints and muscles for training.
  • Build technique before power. Correct stances and alignment protect the knees, hips and back.
  • Train with control. In kumite, techniques are stopped short so that partners stay safe.
  • Listen to your body. Train within your limits, rest when you need to and drink plenty of water.
  • Tell your instructor. Let the instructor know about any injury or health condition before class, so exercises can be adapted.

If you are injured

Stop training and tell an instructor straight away. For minor sprains and strains, rest, gentle ice wrapped in a cloth, light compression and raising the injured area can help in the first day or two. Seek medical advice for anything more than a minor injury, and always for a suspected fracture, a head injury or pain that does not settle. Call 999 in an emergency.

Support at EmptyHands

EmptyHands instructors are trained in first aid, and students are encouraged to report any training problem so that it can be looked after and the lesson shared. Through the EmptyHands Shiatsu clinic, Azeem Sensei also offers advice and Shiatsu to support recovery from sports injuries.

title: Sōtai master class with Rex Lassalle
excerpt: The late Rex Lassalle taught his Be Easy Sōtai method at the EmptyHands dojo: a gentle self-help therapy that moves the body towards ease rather than effort.
html:
The late Rex Lassalle, Shiatsu master, osteopath, Aikidoka and authority on East Asian astrology, visited the EmptyHands dojo in 2024 to teach his Be Easy Sōtai method. It was a privilege to host him. You can read the tribute to Rex here.

What is Sōtai?

Sōtai is a gentle movement therapy developed by the Japanese doctor Keizo Hashimoto (1897-1993) of Sendai. Its name, 操体, deliberately reverses the Japanese word for exercise, taisō (体操). Dr Hashimoto saw Sōtai as an antidote to forceful, regimented exercise: instead of pushing into pain, you move towards what feels easy and comfortable, and let the body rebalance itself.

Rex developed this into Be Easy Sōtai over many years of practice. It uses simple body checks to find movements that feel easy and those that feel difficult or uncomfortable. Small, gentle shifts, repeated regularly, gradually add up to better balance and wellbeing.

The Be Easy Sōtai method

1. Surrender the body

Begin by relaxing. Scan for tension from the crown of the head to the feet, and let the breath slow down as the muscles release.

2. Wake up the senses

Gently stimulate the sense organs, with circular pressure on points around the face:

  • Eyes - move them slowly left and right, then up and down, five times.
  • Nose - move it in all directions and press gently around the nostrils, five times.
  • Lips - tighten and relax them, then circle the mouth clockwise and anticlockwise, five times.
  • Tongue - release it and stretch it left and right, five times.
  • Ears - stimulate the lobes and gently stretch the ears, five times.

3. Test, ease and retest

Use simple tests to find which side of the body holds more tension. Then move five times towards the easy side, and retest to see what has changed:

  • Psoas test - stretch each leg and notice which side feels less comfortable.
  • Hip test - walk slowly or bend left and right to find the side that feels uneasy.
  • Ankle test - rotate and flex the ankles to find the most difficult angle.
  • Wrist test - rotate and flex the wrists in the same way.
  • Neck test - turn the head slowly to find the most difficult position.

The method is simple enough for anyone to try at home. Rex’s message was always the same: health comes through ease, not force. To explore this kind of bodywork, read more about Shiatsu at EmptyHands.

title: The dojo warm-up
excerpt: Why every EmptyHands class starts with a warm-up, what it involves, and how senior students learn to lead it for the junior class.
html:
Every EmptyHands Karate class begins the same way: with a warm-up. It might look like simple exercise, but it is an important part of training, and it is often led by senior students taking the junior class through the routine.

Why warm up?

  • It prevents injury. Raising the heart rate and body temperature prepares muscles, tendons and joints for the work ahead.
  • It improves performance. Warm muscles move faster and more freely, so techniques are sharper.
  • It focuses the mind. The warm-up marks the change from everyday life to training.

A typical warm-up

  1. Raise the pulse - light jogging, skipping or stepping drills for a few minutes.
  2. Mobilise the joints - gentle circles of the neck, shoulders, wrists, hips, knees and ankles.
  3. Dynamic stretches - leg swings, lunges and torso turns that move through the full range used in Karate.
  4. Stances and footwork - moving through zenkutsu-dachi, kiba-dachi and kokutsu-dachi to wake up the legs.
  5. Light kihon - easy punches, blocks and kicks before the main lesson builds up speed and power.

Longer, held stretches are best kept for the end of the class, when the body is fully warm.

Learning to lead

Leading the warm-up is one of the first responsibilities senior students take on. Standing in front of the class builds confidence, teaches them to give clear instructions and helps them look after younger students. It is an early step on the path to instructing, and a reminder that in a dojo everyone learns from one another.

title: Bodhidharma, founder of the martial arts
excerpt: Bodhidharma brought Zen Buddhism to China and, according to legend, taught the Shaolin monks exercises that grew into the martial arts. The story, the legend and his legacy.
html:
Bodhidharma was a Buddhist monk of the 5th or 6th century AD. He is remembered as the founder of Chan Buddhism, known in Japan as Zen, and in martial arts circles as the teacher who brought physical training to the Shaolin Monastery. His story mixes history and legend, but its message has inspired martial artists for centuries.

Early life

Tradition says Bodhidharma came from a royal family in southern India and gave up his title to follow a spiritual path. He studied under the Buddhist teacher Prajñātāra, who sent him to China to spread the teaching. Bodhidharma stressed direct experience and meditation over reliance on scriptures alone.

Journey to China

One famous story tells of his meeting with Emperor Wu of Liang, a devout Buddhist. The emperor asked how much merit he had earned by building temples and supporting monks. Bodhidharma replied: “No merit at all.” Good deeds done for the sake of reward, he explained, bring no true merit. The puzzled emperor let him go, and Bodhidharma travelled north.

He settled near the Shaolin Monastery on Mount Song. Legend says he meditated facing a cave wall for nine years.

Training the Shaolin monks

According to legend, Bodhidharma found the monks too weak to sit through long hours of meditation, so he taught them exercises to strengthen the body and calm the mind. These exercises are said to be the seed of Shaolin Kung Fu.

Historians point out that the link between Bodhidharma and fighting arts first appears in texts written many centuries after his death, so it is best understood as legend. Even so, the idea at its heart, that physical training and meditation support each other, is central to Zen and to the martial arts.

His influence on the martial arts

Zen thinking deeply shaped Japanese martial arts, including Karate, Judo, Kendo and Aikido. Ideas such as mushin (無心, “no mind”), the state of acting clearly and naturally without being caught up in thought, come from the Zen tradition that Bodhidharma founded. Read more in Karate mindsets.

Daruma in Japan

In Japan, Bodhidharma is known as Daruma. The round, red Daruma doll, which rights itself whenever it is knocked over, is a popular symbol of perseverance and good luck. People paint in one eye when they set a goal and the second when they achieve it.

Why his story still matters

Whether history or legend, Bodhidharma’s story reminds martial artists that training is about more than fighting. Strength, discipline, patience and a clear mind are developed together, on the mat and off it. Read more about the history of Karate-Dō.

title: Chi: understanding the vital life force
excerpt: What is Chi? An introduction to the vital life force of Chinese medicine and the martial arts: Yin and Yang, the Five Elements, the vital substances and how to cultivate Chi.
html:
The word Chi (also written Qi, or Ki in Japanese) is used often in martial arts and healing circles. It is usually translated as energy, vital force or life force: the unseen force that, in Chinese thought, flows through all living things and keeps them in balance. This article introduces the main ideas behind it.

Chi and the meridians

In Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM), Chi flows through the body along pathways called meridians, each linked to an organ. Health depends on Chi flowing smoothly; blockages, excess or deficiency are seen as the roots of imbalance and illness. Shiatsu, acupressure, Tai Chi and Chi Kung all work with this flow.

Yin and Yang

Chi always has two complementary sides, Yin and Yang. Yin is quiet, cool and inward; Yang is active, warm and outward. The familiar symbol shows each side containing a seed of the other, and neither is better than the other. As one grows, the other gives way, keeping the whole in balance. These ideas draw on very old Chinese thought, including the I Ching (Book of Changes), whose oldest parts date back nearly 3,000 years.

The Five Elements

The theory of the Five Elements (Wu Xing) describes how Chi changes and moves through five phases: Wood, Fire, Earth, Metal and Water. The theory took shape more than 2,000 years ago and remains central to TCM. The elements relate to one another in two cycles:

  • The supporting cycle - Wood feeds Fire, Fire creates Earth (ash), Earth bears Metal, Metal carries Water, and Water nourishes Wood.
  • The controlling cycle - Wood parts Earth, Earth dams Water, Water puts out Fire, Fire melts Metal, and Metal cuts Wood.

Each element has a Yin and a Yang organ. Metal, for example, pairs the Lungs (Yin) with the Large Intestine (Yang). Their meridians form linked pathways of Yin and Yang energy circulating through the body.

The vital substances

TCM describes the body’s health through three linked systems:

  • The vital substances - Qi (energy), Xue (blood), Jinye (body fluids), Jing (essence) and Shen (spirit).
  • The Zang Fu - the Yin and Yang organs described above.
  • The Jing Luo - the meridians that connect the organs and carry the vital substances.

Chi is said to have five main functions in the body:

  • Moving - circulating blood and body fluids.
  • Warming - keeping the body and limbs warm.
  • Protecting - defending against outside influences such as colds.
  • Holding - keeping fluids and organs in their proper place.
  • Transforming - turning food and drink into energy and blood.

Cultivating Chi

In the martial arts, Chi is cultivated through practice. When a student performs a form or kata, or holds a Chi Kung posture with correct alignment, relaxed breathing and calm attention, they are said to cultivate Chi. Over time, a deeper study of the internal martial arts shows how this relaxed, connected strength can be used in self-defence.

title: Yoga and Karate
excerpt: Breath, posture and a calm mind: how Yoga and Karate complement each other, from Prana and Chi to postures that mirror Karate stances and kicks.
html:
Yoga and Karate may look very different, but they share a great deal. Both join breath, posture and focus, and both aim for a calm, balanced mind. This article looks at how the two practices complement each other.

Prana and Chi

In Karate and the Chinese arts we often talk about Chi (Qi), the life force that moves through the body along the meridians. Yoga has a similar idea: prana, the life force that flows through channels called nadis. Both traditions teach that when this energy flows freely, body and mind are healthy and at ease.

A shared history

Tradition tells of the Indian monk Bodhidharma, who travelled to China and taught the Shaolin monks exercises to strengthen the body for long hours of meditation. Whatever the history behind the legend, it reflects a real connection: in both Yoga and the martial arts, physical training is a path to a calmer, clearer mind. Yoga’s principle of ahimsa, non-violence, also finds an echo in Karate, the “empty hand” that seeks to avoid conflict.

The importance of breath

The breathing practices of Yoga are called pranayama. Notice how your breath changes when you face a difficult situation: it becomes short and heavy, compared with the slow, relaxed breath of a calm day. Pranayama trains us to slow and lengthen the breath, which in turn calms the mind.

Yoga teaches that the body must first be strong and steady in its postures (asana) before it can hold the breath well. Karate works in the same way, building the body through stances and kata and developing strength in the hara, the body’s centre below the navel.

Similar practices

  • Meditation - Karate classes begin and end with mokuso, focused breathing while kneeling in seiza. A Yoga session often starts seated in sukhasana, eyes closed, settling into the present moment.
  • Standing still - Tadasana (mountain pose) teaches grounding and weight distribution. It is close to the natural stance of Karate and to Wu Chi in Tai Chi, where weight rests on the balls of the feet over the Bubbling Spring point (KI1).
  • Rising arms - Tiryaka tadasana (swaying palm tree pose) stretches the arms and sides much like the rising block, age uke, found in the Heian kata.
  • Square hips - three-legged downward dog (tri pada adho mukha svanasana) lengthens the spine and opens the hips, and teaches the square hips a karateka needs for balance.
  • Kicking line - virabhadrasana III (warrior 3), with the arms forward and one leg pushing back, mirrors the line of a back kick, ushiro geri.
  • Sequences - the Sun Salutation (surya namaskar) is a series of movements repeated in order, just like a kata. In both, the breath leads the movement.

One aim

Both practices build balance, strength and flexibility, help energy flow freely, and lead towards calm, confidence and fluid movement. Above all, both train the mind. As the Buddha taught, the path to peace lies in mental discipline.

title: Training Karate online through the pandemic
excerpt: A senior EmptyHands student reflects on lockdown, a trip to Japan, a Zen dragon and why it is okay not to be okay, and what Karate taught them about honesty and routine.
html:
A personal reflection written by a senior EmptyHands student during the first Coronavirus lockdown in 2020.

Life under lockdown

The pandemic changed our lives in countless ways. Adjusting to lockdown took a real toll on mental health. News updates reported the latest figures every day, and it was easy to feel lost. People were cut off from friends and family, stockpiling toilet paper (yes, we know you’re out there) and facing the uncertainty of not knowing when it would end.

I struggled too, with the effect on my studies, my Karate and my work. Here are some reflections drawn from what I know about mental health, my Karate journey and my own experience. I hope you take away one idea and try it. If not, I hope you at least enjoy the read.

The dragon on the ceiling

I love to travel, and I have a tradition of bringing home a piece of art from every new city. It must have a unique story or capture an interesting moment. When I went to Japan the year before lockdown, my expectations were high.

One morning I visited a temple to practise Zen meditation with the monks. The head abbot led me into the meditation hall, and the first thing I saw was a huge dragon painted across the whole ceiling. Its eyes seemed to follow me everywhere, not in a creepy way, but like a judgemental parent. When I asked what it meant, the abbot said: “The dragon represents the true nature of Zen. It asks you who your true self is when you strip back all the layers.” I knew I had to find that dragon and bring it home.

Who is your true self?

Look at the dragon. Look at its eyes, and ask yourself who your true self is. It is a question I pondered all through lockdown, when there wasn’t much else to do. We lost the freedom to travel, and life went on without restaurants, workplaces or dojos.

So ask yourself honestly: how have you coped? Have you been productive, or is there an imprint in the sofa from days of Netflix and junk food? The dragon is watching, so be truthful.

In April my Sensei told me: “Think of a martial arts project you would love to pursue but never had time for. Now is your chance!” I promised to write loads of articles. Two months later, this is my first. I tell you this because facing our own truths matters, even when they make us look less than perfect.

Honest with ourselves

Martial artists are used to looking at their weaknesses. Kata can always improve, stances can always be stronger and kicks can always be higher. So when I reflect on my lack of productivity in lockdown, I can say it plainly: I can do better. I feel the dragon judging me.

The comfort of routine

Having something stable in your life is a wonderful thing. I have trained in Karate for over 13 years, and one constant through the pandemic was my Karate lessons. Every Thursday evening, whatever else happened, we logged in to the online dojo and trained together. It connected us and grounded us.

In Japan I also visited a Budo centre to try Kendo. The dojo was beautiful, with sliding doors on all four sides opening onto a courtyard. Unsure of the etiquette, I lingered at the entrance while a class finished. After training at the JKA headquarters, where strict etiquette is always expected, I didn’t want to get it wrong.

When the class ended, the woman the instructor had been demonstrating on took off her men, the Kendo helmet, smiled and welcomed me in. She was the instructor’s wife, and she handled the dojo’s administration as well as teaching alongside him. I felt instantly at ease, and only later understood why: my own dojo is run the same way, by Sensei and his wife. That sense of familiarity is precious, and in lockdown we all had to find it somewhere, whether in online training or video calls with friends.

It’s okay not to be okay

One lesson stood out: it is okay not to be okay. It is fine to have days when you just want to sit and do nothing. I was raised to believe that a day doing nothing is a day wasted. But finishing a six-pack of doughnuts in front of the TV from morning till night is definitely not nothing, thank you very much!

Jokes aside, this may be the only time in our lives when circumstances forced us to stop. So why the pressure to learn a language, bake bread or exercise every day? Mindfulness is the practice of being fully present, even while doing nothing. My favourite is sitting on my balcony at sunset, imagining myself standing on the clouds and performing my favourite kata. Try it: kata on a cloud is fun.

Coming home from Japan

When I returned to the dojo after Japan, Sensei said: “I bet you’re feeling motivated and inspired! I know I did after my trip.” I nodded and said, “Oss, Sensei.” But inside I felt deflated. In Japan, Karate truly was a way of life: the standard of the students, the camaraderie, the culture. Then I came home to the news that the last of the classmates I had trained with towards black belt had left. When I taught, I didn’t see the enthusiasm I had seen in Japan. I wanted to go back.

Months later I understood. I had loved Japan so much because I had lived the dream I’d always had: training with masters and sitting with monks. That chapter was complete, and I needed new inspiration.

Find a new goal

My challenge to you is to find something that inspires you and make it your goal. Dream big, because big dreams are the ones that change our lives. I am still working out my own next aspiration. Sensei always says: “I can open the door for you, but it’s up to you to walk through it.” He has opened many doors, and I have not walked through as many as I wanted to. I feel the dragon staring at me. I guess I have something else to reflect on.

Final thoughts

I found this article hard to write. I first planned to give the usual advice: sleep well, eat healthily, avoid stress. But that wasn’t what helped me. What helped was being honest with myself, holding on to familiar routines like Thursday training, and allowing myself to rest. Whatever helps you, look after yourself, stay connected to your dojo, and remember the dragon. Oss.

title: Fight Club: back to the roots of Karate
excerpt: The EmptyHands Fight Club returns to the roots of Karate in Okinawan tō-de, training practical self-defence while keeping the mental and moral side of the art.
html:
The EmptyHands Fight Club goes back to the roots of Karate to explore how traditional techniques work in practical self-defence today. This article explains where those roots lie and what the Fight Club sets out to do.

The roots of Karate

Karate grew from an older art practised in the Ryukyu Islands, now known as Okinawa. Sitting between Japan and China, the islands were a crossroads of trade and culture. Local fighting methods blended with Chinese martial arts to form tō-de (唐手), often called “Tang hand” or “Chinese hand”, sometimes known as tō-de jutsu.

In the early 20th century, the art was formalised and taught more widely, with standard training methods and, later, belt grades. It became known as Karate and spread worldwide, giving rise to styles such as Shotokan, Goju-Ryu and Shito-Ryu. Read more about the history of Karate-Dō.

What the Fight Club does

The Fight Club explores the practical, self-defence side of Karate:

  • Realistic scenarios - applying traditional techniques to the kinds of situations people may face today.
  • Bunkai - drawing practical applications from kata. Read more about bunkai.
  • Pressure-testing - checking techniques against a resisting partner, safely and with control.
  • Mental resilience - staying calm, aware and decisive under pressure.

Tradition and modern life

The Fight Club is not about aggression. The aim is to adapt the teachings of the old masters to modern needs while keeping the values that make Karate a way of life: respect, self-control and avoiding conflict wherever possible. Practitioners of every level are welcome, and the training builds confidence as well as skill.

Wisdom from Gichin Funakoshi

Gichin Funakoshi, the father of modern Karate, urged his students to study the past to understand the present:

“To search for the old is to understand the new. The old, the new, this is a matter of time. In all things one must have a clear mind. The Way: who will pass it on straight and well?”

Understanding where Karate comes from makes it easier to use it well today, and to pass it on to the next generation. Interested in self-defence? Ask about the Self-Defence Scenarios workshops or book a trial Karate class.

title: Boosting immunity with acupressure
excerpt: Three traditional acupressure points, Kidney 27, Lung 7 and Large Intestine 11, used in Chinese medicine to support the body during colds and flu, and how to find them.
html:
Traditional Chinese Medicine has used acupressure for centuries to help the body stay balanced and resist illness. This article describes three points that are traditionally used to support the immune system, especially during cold and flu season, and how to find them yourself.

Please note: acupressure is a complementary practice and does not replace medical advice. If you feel unwell, have a high temperature or symptoms that are getting worse, contact your GP or NHS 111.

How to use acupressure

Use the pad of your thumb or finger to apply firm but comfortable pressure, or small circles, for one to two minutes on each side. Breathe slowly and relax while you press.

Kidney 27 (Shufu)

Where: in the hollow just below the collarbone, about two thumb-widths either side of the centre line of the chest.

Traditional use: Kidney 27 is traditionally used for chest and breathing problems, such as coughs and shortness of breath, and for tiredness. In TCM the Kidneys “grasp” the Qi of the Lungs, helping the breath reach deep into the body.

Lung 7 (Lieque)

Where: on the thumb side of the forearm, about two finger-widths above the wrist crease. To find it, interlace the thumbs and index fingers of both hands: the tip of the top index finger rests in a small groove above the wrist bone. That groove is Lung 7.

Traditional use: Lung 7 is one of the main points for coughs, sore throats and the early stages of a cold. It is also used for headaches and a stiff neck, and is said to strengthen the body’s defensive Qi.

Large Intestine 11 (Quchi)

Where: at the outer end of the elbow crease when the elbow is bent.

Traditional use: Large Intestine 11 is traditionally used to “clear heat”, so it is often included for fever and sore throats during colds and flu. It is also a key point for the elbow and arm, and is one of the elbow points that open in Tai Chi and Chi Kung when the elbows sink.

Looking after yourself

Acupressure works best alongside healthy habits: a balanced diet rich in fruit and vegetables, plenty of water, good sleep, regular exercise and ways of managing stress. Gentle movement practices such as Tai Chi and Chi Kung support all of these.
