title: Kobudō: traditional weapons of Okinawa
excerpt: Kobudō means "old martial way". For karateka it usually means the traditional weapons of Okinawa, such as the bō, sai, tonfa and nunchaku, studied alongside empty-hand Karate.
html:
Kobudō (古武道) means “old martial way”. In mainland Japan the word describes the classical martial traditions of the samurai, such as swordsmanship. In the Karate world, it usually means Okinawan kobudō: the traditional weapons studied alongside empty-hand Karate.

Where it comes from

Okinawan kobudō developed over centuries in the Ryukyu Kingdom, alongside the empty-hand art that became Karate. A popular story says that Okinawan farmers and fishermen turned their everyday tools into weapons when ordinary weapons were restricted. Historians think the reality is more mixed, with much of the art developed and preserved by Okinawa’s warrior class, but many kobudō weapons do resemble farming and fishing tools.

In the 20th century, masters such as Taira Shinken worked to collect and preserve the old weapon kata, and today kobudō is practised around the world.

The main weapons

  • Bō (棒) - a long wooden staff, about six feet (1.8 metres) long. It is used for striking, blocking and thrusting, and teaches control of distance.
  • Sai (釵) - a metal truncheon with two curved side prongs. It is used for blocking, trapping and striking, and teaches angles and timing.
  • Tonfa (トンファー) - a wooden baton with a side handle, which can spin and strike or guard the forearm.
  • Nunchaku (ヌンチャク) - two short sticks joined by a cord, demanding speed, coordination and fluid movement.
  • Kama (鎌) - a short sickle, usually trained with practice blades for safety.
  • Eku (櫂) - an oar, used much like a staff.

Shorter staffs such as the jō are also widely practised in Japanese arts such as Jōdō.

How kobudō is trained

Like Karate, kobudō is learned through kihon (basic techniques), kata (set forms) and partner drills. Each weapon has its own kata, which build muscle memory, precision, timing and awareness of distance. The weapon becomes an extension of the body, so the same principles of stance, posture and hip movement apply as in empty-hand Karate.

Why practise it?

  • Better Karate - weapons training sharpens distance, timing and body mechanics.
  • Coordination - handling a weapon with both hands challenges the brain and body.
  • Focus and discipline - weapons demand full attention and respect for safety.
  • Connection with history - kobudō keeps alive the traditions Karate grew from.

Above all, kobudō shares Karate’s deeper aims: respect, discipline and self-improvement. Read more about Budō culture, or try learning a staff form as a way to train the brain.

title: Coping with stress: is Karate the answer?
excerpt: An EmptyHands black belt and mental health practitioner explains how kumite, kata and mokuso meditation help with stress, with a simple five-step exercise to try today.
html:
Written by a senior EmptyHands student who works in mental health.

Have you ever had one of those days? You’re running late, squeezing onto an overcrowded train, holding on to what little calm you have left as you finish your third coffee. That is what stress looks like, and it can show up as poor sleep, headaches or a short temper.

Why we need ways to cope

Stress is widespread, especially among young people. In a 2018 survey of 1,000 18 to 25-year-olds, the charity UK Youth found that they spent more than six hours a day feeling stressed or worried. We all need healthy ways to cope, and Karate can be one of them.

My journey

I started Karate at the age of ten, and over twelve years it has become a central part of my life. I joined the instructing programme early, which meant explaining techniques to students and answering their questions. That gave me a deeper understanding of Karate and its principles.

Today I work with people facing mental health difficulties, creating intervention plans and providing therapy. Many of the lessons I draw on come straight from the dojo.

Kumite: calm under pressure

Karate training rests on three foundations: kihon (basics), kata (forms) and kumite (sparring). Kumite builds timing and accuracy, but more importantly it teaches us to manage the fight-or-flight response.

Imagine looking up from this article to see someone standing in front of you with a knife. Your heart races and your brain scrambles to decide: run, freeze or fight? That is fight or flight, the body’s automatic response to danger.

Regular, controlled sparring gets us used to adrenaline and quick decisions, so the response becomes familiar rather than overwhelming. Over time it develops instinct and calm, which help in stressful moments far from the dojo.

Kata: moving meditation

Once a kata begins, you give it your full attention. Kata also trains the breath: some movements need a strong exhalation, others are slow and deliberate. This combination of focus, breathing and set movement makes kata a form of moving meditation.

When I first learned a kata and felt pleased with my performance, Sensei said: “Okay, now do it ten more times!” It frustrated me then, but I now see the value of that repetition. In daily life our senses are in overdrive, with one eye on the TV, one ear on the phone and our minds on tomorrow. Practising the same movements again and again gives the mind a rare chance to rest on one thing.

The importance of balance

After graduating, I found it hard to balance work and life, and I cut back on sleep and meals. Healthy habits such as sleep, regular meals and exercise are essential for a healthy mind.

A Shiatsu master once suggested I build small rituals to separate work from home, such as changing my clothes when I get in. A ritual like this marks the change from one activity to the next, so the mind is not scattered across everything at once.

Mokuso: the power of stillness

Every EmptyHands class begins with the same ritual: we light incense, ring a bell and meditate. This is mokuso, Japanese for meditation. The sounds and smells help us focus, and our busy minds slow down for a moment.

I once worked with a client who had severe anxiety and panic attacks and felt he had tried everything. My Karate experience told me how powerful simple meditation can be, so I included these steps in his plan:

  1. Space - find a quiet, comfortable room at a pleasant temperature, free from interruptions and not too dark or bright.
  2. Posture - sit comfortably, close your eyes, relax your shoulders and keep your back straight.
  3. Breathing - breathe deeply in through your nose and slowly out through your mouth, again and again.
  4. Focus - concentrate only on your breathing. When your mind wanders to an itch or what to have for dinner, gently bring it back to the breath. A calming scent, such as incense, can help.
  5. Feeling - notice the signs that stress is easing: muscles relaxing and thoughts becoming clearer.

It sounds simple, but ask yourself: when did you last sit quietly and think of nothing?

Calm that comes from training

On a counselling course, we practised being both therapist and client. When my partner began crying as she shared her story, my tutor noticed how calm I stayed. That calm did not come from nowhere. It came from years of kata, of meeting the unexpected in kumite, and of sitting in mokuso.

Gichin Funakoshi, the father of modern Karate, taught that Karate goes beyond the dojo and into everyday life. Its lessons can help us all to cope.

A challenge for today

Take five minutes today to try the exercise above. And if you would like to go further, find a dojo that values this kind of traditional training. Book a trial Karate class, or read about Karate mindsets.

If stress or anxiety is affecting your daily life, please talk to your GP, or contact NHS 111 or the Samaritans on 116 123.

title: Five ways to become a better karateka
excerpt: Five simple resolutions for your Karate training - ease, joy, challenge, dream and change - with practical steps to help you improve at any grade.
html:
Whether it’s a new year or a new term, here are five simple resolutions to help you get more from your Karate training.

1. Ease: break it down

Think about the hardest part of your training, then break it into smaller techniques or drills. Nobody climbs a mountain before climbing a hill. If a kata or kumite drill is giving you trouble, start with the parts you find easy. Often a task is only partly difficult, but the hard part clouds our view of the simple steps that lead to it.

2. Joy: find what you love

Enjoyment is what keeps us going. Find your favourite part of Karate, whatever it is, and make it your starting point. Explore it more deeply, then use it to step outside your comfort zone. Be playful, and ask fellow karateka and instructors for feedback. If you are not enjoying training, talk to someone.

3. Challenge: face what you avoid

We all have things we would rather not do, and we are very good at avoiding them. Some students avoid kumite or kata; others avoid stamina training or reading about the theory of Karate. If the “don’t like” list grows longer than the “like” list, we know how the story ends.

Karate may be one of the hardest things you ever do, but also one of the most rewarding. Think back to something that was a struggle at first, like riding a bike. You overcame fear and doubt by challenging yourself. Look for the fun in what feels like hard work: train with a friend, attend extra classes, or ask an instructor whether they faced the same struggle.

4. Dream: set your goal

Why did you start Karate? And what brings you back every week? What is your highest goal in Karate? It can be anything. Write it down, so it lives on paper rather than weighing on your mind. That is the first step to making it real. In Budō we reach for what seems out of reach.

5. Change: break a habit

Change is the thing we avoid most. Why change something that works, or something that feels easy? But for knowledge to grow, our attitude to training has to keep developing. Pick one bad habit, however small, and set out to change it:

  1. Write down the one thing you would like to change in your training.
  2. Write three simple steps to achieve it.
  3. Talk it through with a friend or instructor.
  4. Choose a date and time to start, so it becomes real.

Good luck, and remember to practise Karate for its own sake.

“Karate-do is definitely a martial way, and its identity lies in dō, or principles. Any martial art without proper training of the mind turns into beastly behaviour.” - Shōshin Nagamine

For more ideas, read Karate rules for personal growth.

title: Neurobics for Karate
excerpt: Neurobics means exercising the brain by using all the senses in new ways. Karate is full of neurobic exercises, from kata on the other side to training with your eyes closed.
html:
Have you ever wondered which exercises are best for the brain? Many people think studying is the only way to keep the mind sharp. But some scientists believe that one of the best ways to exercise the brain is to use all your senses, sight, sound, touch, taste and smell, in new and unexpected ways.

What is neurobics?

The term “neurobics” was coined by the American neurobiologist Lawrence Katz and the writer Manning Rubin in their 1999 book Keep Your Brain Alive. Katz suggested that much mental decline comes not from losing brain cells but from weaker connections between them, and that breaking routines and engaging the senses in unusual ways can encourage new connections.

The ideas are popular rather than proven, and neurobics is not a way to raise your IQ. The aim is simply to keep the mind active and fit. And Karate, it turns out, is full of neurobic exercises.

Neurobic exercises in Karate

Switch sides

Using your non-dominant side makes the brain work harder. Most kata begin to the left; try performing your kata starting to the right.

Train with your eyes closed

Doing a familiar task without sight forces the brain to use different pathways. Next time you are in the dojo, try a kata with your eyes closed, in a safe space with room around you.

Learn a weapon

Ask your Sensei about staff training, such as Jōdō or the bō from kobudō. Handling a weapon with both hands develops the senses in the fingers and hands and challenges coordination.

Reverse it

Doing things backwards makes you think about every step, which also helps you break a technique down. Practise a sequence in reverse, or try a backward roll after a forward one.

Say it out loud

Read or recite the Dojo Kun or Funakoshi’s twenty precepts (Niju Kun) aloud. Reading, speaking and hearing the words engage different parts of the brain at once.

Map it out

Draw a map of the last kata you learned, showing every turn and step, or create a short routine of your own just for fun.

Take a new route

Much of what we do runs on autopilot. Take a different route to the dojo, or try something new, such as eating with chopsticks in your other hand.

Talk to people

Conversation engages many senses at once, yet in the digital age we often text instead of talking. Make the dojo a device-free space: talk with fellow karateka and instructors, ask questions, and get to know people with different interests, including martial artists from other styles.

Try something new, and do it the hard way

New experiences stimulate the brain. If training starts to feel stale, tell your Sensei: a new kata or drill can reignite your interest. Watch other martial artists, pick something you admire and practise it. And resist the shortcut sometimes: instead of a quick video, read a book on Karate history or ask a senior student.

Meditation and movement

Of all mental exercises, meditation may be the hardest. Research suggests it can reduce stress and improve focus, attention and mood, which is why every class includes mokuso. Kata, mindfulness and Chi Kung are forms of meditation too.

Regular physical training helps the brain as well, lifting mood and reducing stress. Karate has many dimensions beyond kicking and punching, so explore them, ask your instructors for ideas, and see what you discover about yourself.

title: Karate mindsets
excerpt: Six states of mind rooted in Zen that guide Karate training: mushotoku, hishiryō, zanshin, fudōshin, mushin and satori, and how each one shows up in the dojo.
html:
Karate trains the mind as much as the body. This article describes six states of mind, rooted in the practice of Zen meditation (zazen), that can guide your training and your daily life.

1. Mushotoku: training without seeking reward

Mushotoku is a state of mind in which you act without seeking results and give without expecting anything in return. Most of what we do is for a reward: a qualification, a grade or a certificate. The belt system gives Karate a clear structure, but if the next belt becomes the only reason to train, learning is limited from the start.

Mushotoku means letting go of that attachment, so you can discover something new about yourself. It grows only through regular, persistent training. Next time you put on your gi, remind yourself that the aim is to understand yourself, not to collect achievements. The Zen teacher Taisen Deshimaru wrote about this idea in Mushotoku Mind.

2. Hishiryō: thinking without thinking

During training, thoughts and distractions come and go. Hishiryō is the state of letting thoughts pass without following them. It can sound strange, but it is essential for every karateka.

We often overthink moves and drills, creating conflict in the mind that stops us finding the essence of a movement. Accept movements for what they are: not everything needs deep analysis. Zen teachers say this peaceful state is the mind’s original condition.

3. Zanshin: the remaining mind

Zanshin means “remaining mind”: total awareness of your surroundings, fully present in the here and now. It is the alertness you keep after a technique, ready for whatever comes next.

Regular kihon, kata and kumite, together with meditation and focused breathing, develop alertness and sensitivity, so you respond to pressure more calmly. Over time zanshin spreads into daily life, on the way to school or work or over breakfast, reminding us that no moment is ordinary.

4. Fudōshin: the immovable mind

Fudōshin means “immovable mind”: a calm, steady state that stays undisturbed by fear, pain or stress. The samurai prized it, and it is often seen in experienced martial artists.

Several stances and kata express this quality in their very names:

  • Fudō-dachi (不動立ち, “immovable stance”), also called sōchin-dachi after the kata Sōchin.
  • Sanchin-dachi (三戦立ち), named after the Goju-Ryu kata Sanchin, “three battles”.
  • Seiyunchin, a Goju-Ryu kata of pulling and control, practised with a calm, settled mind.
  • Hangetsu (半月, “half moon”), an advanced Shotokan kata that shares much with Sanchin.

Fudōshin is a determined, peaceful state of mind that doubt and fear cannot shake. It can only be built through steady practice and hard work.

5. Mushin: no mind

Mushin means “no mind”: a mind free from fixation on any thought, distraction or emotion. Without ego or impulse, there is only clarity and presence.

A mushin mind is not empty; it is fully aware. It is like muddy water after heavy rain: once the mud settles, the water becomes clear, and the sun is reflected on its surface.

Mushin can take years to develop. A simple test in the dojo is to have a partner attack you at random, under supervision and with control, and notice your reactions. In training, the mind must stay free from anger, fear and judgement.

6. Satori: awakening

Satori is awakening: a sudden flash of insight or complete understanding. It cannot be explained, only experienced.

People often treat satori as something special or a final goal. In fact it is about returning the mind to its original, simple state. Every karateka begins as a white belt with an empty mind; as the years pass and kata and drills pile up, keeping that simplicity becomes harder. Satori reminds us of where we began.

Perhaps we glimpse satori more often than we realise, but our busy lives stop us noticing. It comes through good posture, steady practice and surrendering fully to the present moment, free from fear.

Continue with neurobics for Karate or coping with stress.

title: The Shotokan tiger
excerpt: The story of the Shotokan tiger, drawn by the painter Hōan Kosugi for Gichin Funakoshi, and what its brushstrokes and circle mean for karateka today.
html:
The tiger inside a circle is the best-known symbol of Shotokan Karate. It appears on badges, gi and dojo walls around the world. Here is where it came from, and what it can teach us.

Where the tiger came from

The tiger was painted by Hōan Kosugi, a well-known Japanese artist and a friend and student of Gichin Funakoshi, the father of modern Karate. Kosugi encouraged Funakoshi to put his teaching into a book, and drew the tiger for its cover. Funakoshi’s first book, Ryūkyū Kenpō: Karate, was published in 1922, and the tiger has been linked with his teaching ever since.

The idea came from an old Japanese expression, tora no maki, the “tiger scroll”: a book of essential teachings. The tiger also suggests the qualities Karate builds: strength, power and tenacity.

An unfinished tiger

Look closely and you will see that the tiger is not fully outlined. Its brushstrokes suggest the body without completing it. At EmptyHands we read this as a reminder that Karate is a complete system with many parts: stances, strikes, kicks, blocks, joint locks, pressure points, takedowns and controlling techniques. Neglect any one of them, and the whole is weakened.

The four pillars

We also see in the tiger the four pillars every class works through:

  • Kihon (basics) - the stances and techniques everything else is built on.
  • Kata (forms) - set sequences that hand down the techniques and strategies of the masters.
  • Bunkai (application) - taking kata apart to discover their practical self-defence.
  • Kumite (sparring) - applying techniques with a partner, safely and with control.

The circle: containing power

The circle around the tiger can be read as Funakoshi’s vision for Karate: power held within limits. Training gives real strength and skill, which must never be used impulsively or recklessly, only to defend yourself or protect those who cannot protect themselves.

The spirit of the tiger

Over the years, too many students give up their training because they never connect with the true spirit of Karate. Training with the right mindset makes all the difference, especially when times are hard.

These EmptyHands students kept training all the way through the lockdown period. They never gave up, and they showed the resilience and strength the Shotokan tiger stands for. Read more about the history of Karate-Dō.

title: Evidence-based Karate training
excerpt: Medicine and education rely on evidence-based practice. How Karate can use sports science for conditioning, injury prevention and mental skills while keeping its traditions.
html:
Evidence-based practice means combining the best available research with professional experience to decide what works. It has transformed medicine, education and sport. Martial arts have been slower to adopt it, and Karate has much to gain.

What is evidence-based practice?

At its heart, evidence-based practice is a cycle of asking questions: what works, what doesn’t, and why? Doctors use research to choose the most effective treatments. Teachers use it to choose methods that help students learn. In each case, decisions rest on evidence as well as habit and tradition.

Martial arts training has traditionally relied on techniques and methods passed down from teacher to student. These traditions are valuable, but they are rarely tested in the way other fields expect. Evidence-based training can bridge that gap without losing what makes the art special.

Where Karate can benefit

Strength and conditioning

Kata and kumite need strength, speed and endurance as well as skill. Sports science offers proven ways to build these, from targeted strength work to interval training, so that conditioning supports technique directly.

Injury prevention and recovery

Martial arts carry a risk of injury to joints, muscles and bones. Research-backed mobility work, warm-ups and recovery help students train for longer. For example, studies suggest that dynamic stretching is better than long static stretches before training, which is why the EmptyHands warm-up keeps longer holds for the end of class. Read more about sports injuries and the martial arts.

Mental skills

Visualisation, meditation and techniques from cognitive behavioural approaches can improve focus, reduce anxiety and help performance under pressure. They fit naturally with the mental discipline already at the heart of Karate. Read coping with stress: is Karate the answer?

Respecting tradition

Evidence-based training does not mean throwing away tradition. It means asking why a technique works as well as how to perform it, staying up to date with research in sports science, biomechanics and psychology, and being open to learning from experts in those fields.

Combining centuries of martial wisdom with modern knowledge gives students a safer, more effective path to mastery, and helps them become well-rounded, skilled and thoughtful karateka.

title: Budō culture
excerpt: Budō, the "martial way", is about far more than fighting. A look at its history, its ethical code and the dojo, health and spiritual rituals that make up Budō culture.
html:
Budō (武道) means “martial way”, from bu (martial) and dō (way). It covers the Japanese martial arts, including Karate-Dō, Judo, Kendo, Aikido and Jōdō. The aim of every Budō is the same: to develop the whole person and to restore balance and harmony.

What is Budō culture?

Budō culture is the set of behaviours, rituals, traditions and beliefs that surround martial arts practice. Practitioners of Budō seek something deeper than routine or reward, and their commitment to personal growth and ethical conduct enables them to contribute to society.

Budō is often misunderstood as a combat sport built on aggression and the pursuit of medals. In truth, because martial arts can be dangerous, they rest on a strong ethical code. Bushidō, the “way of the warrior”, calls for courtesy, sincerity, loyalty, discipline and courage. These values keep training safe, keep egos in check as students face fear and pain, and help resolve conflict before it starts.

A brief history

  • Zen roots - tradition says Bodhidharma brought Chan (Zen) Buddhism to China in the 6th century, and with it the link between meditation and physical training at the Shaolin Monastery.
  • Okinawa and China - from the late 1300s the Ryukyu Kingdom traded closely with China, exchanging goods, ideas and martial arts. This exchange shaped the art that became Karate.
  • The samurai - the samurai rose to power from the 12th century, and their classical martial traditions, known as koryū (古流, “old schools”), were developed for the battlefield. Modern Budō grew from these roots and is still passed on from teacher to student today.

Examples of Budō culture

Dojo rituals

  • Removing shoes before entering the dojo, out of respect and to keep the space clean.
  • Bowing on entering and leaving the dojo, to teachers and to training partners.
  • Paying respect to teachers and those who came before.
  • Wearing the traditional uniform, such as the gi.
  • Studying classic texts such as Miyamoto Musashi’s Book of Five Rings, Sun Tzu’s Art of War and the Bubishi.

Health and wellbeing

  • Finding ikigai, a sense of purpose, and living a balanced, healthy life.
  • The tea ceremony and the lighting of incense.
  • Shiatsu and the study of traditional medicine, such as the Yellow Emperor’s Classic of Internal Medicine.

Spiritual practice

  • Zazen (seated meditation) and mokuso, the meditation at the start and end of every class.
  • Zen gardens and the study of Zen philosophy.
  • Learning from the lives and teachings of the masters.
  • Sumi-e, Japanese ink painting.

Budō culture brings together physical training, ethical conduct, history and spiritual practice. Together they make up the way of the warrior. Read more about Karate mindsets and kobudō.

title: Creating an online dojo with Microsoft Teams
excerpt: How EmptyHands built an online dojo in Microsoft Teams during lockdown: the four dimensions of dojo learning, and practical tips for any martial arts school going online.
html:
Running a dojo during social distancing was a challenge, but the idea of learning online is not new. This article explains how EmptyHands built its online dojo, and offers tips for any martial arts school thinking of doing the same.

Learning at a distance

Distance learning dates back to the 1800s, when teachers taught by post. Computer-based learning began in the 1960s, the internet and home computers brought interactive learning in the 1980s and 1990s, and by the 2000s broadband connected people around the world. Today video platforms have made online learning part of everyday life, and working and studying from home have become normal.

Can martial arts be taught online?

For years I asked that question with doubt. Then lockdown left no choice, and I ran my first class on the best platform I could find. Martial arts teach us that if you commit to something, you go all the way.

Many people think of online learning as a video call with lots of participants. That is only the surface. Live classes are just one part of what an online dojo can offer.

My first experience of martial arts online came long before social media. When I launched the ZenKarate online magazine and forum in 1999, martial artists around the world responded and it built a readership of more than 1,000. It taught me that an online space lets like-minded people share ideas and work together at any time, from anywhere.

The four dimensions of dojo learning

Start by looking at how you already teach. Most dojo learning happens in four ways, and each can be recreated online:

  1. Live practice - the weekly class, led by the instructor. Online, this becomes a scheduled video meeting.
  2. Study and self-practice - the syllabus, kata notes and videos students work on between lessons, shared in one organised place.
  3. Feedback and discussion - questions, corrections and conversation with instructors and fellow students, through channels and chat.
  4. Progress and assessment - tasks, homework and preparation for gradings, tracked so that everyone can see what to work on next.

Tips for building your online dojo in Teams

  • Keep it simple. Don’t overcomplicate your team.
  • Create relevant channels for your classes and the areas of training you focus on, such as kata, kumite or gradings.
  • Use apps within Teams. For example, add the Planner app to a channel to set and track study tasks for students.
  • Focus on what is possible, not on the constraints.

What online learning taught us

Online learning gives students more responsibility for their own training. In the dojo, students can grow used to being led by the teacher, and learning can become automatic, without reflection. Online, students have to ask questions and research for themselves, while still being guided when needed.

I will always be a traditionalist: the true transmission of a martial art happens in person, between teacher and student. But we live in a changing world, and martial arts have adapted to their practitioners many times over the centuries. Read about the EmptyHands Virtual Dojo.

title: Karate rules for personal growth
excerpt: Eleven simple rules, drawn from the teachings of the Karate masters, to help you train better and carry the lessons of the dojo into school, work and daily life.
html:
Karate is about far more than physical technique. The masters spoke of a deeper side to training that shapes the way we think and live. Here are eleven rules, drawn from their teachings, to guide your journey.

“The true science of martial arts means practising them in such a way that they will be useful at any time, and to teach them in such a way that they will be useful in all things.” - Miyamoto Musashi

1. Practise regularly

Practise whenever you have spare time. Regular training builds strong connections with each movement and turns good practice into habit. Over time, the discipline you build in the dojo spills into your studies and work.

2. Practise one thing at a time

It is fine to work on several techniques or kata in a session, but keep your attention on one thing at a time. Focus on a specific technique or drill instead of trying to cover too much at once.

3. Keep it simple

Whatever you are learning, break it down and simplify the movement. Stay true to your kihon and bunkai, and don’t overcomplicate a technique or its application. Remember that there are layers of application, from simple to advanced.

4. Visualise your opponent

All practice must have a context. When you practise a new drill or strike, ask yourself: would this really work? Test it safely with a partner. Visualisation is a powerful tool, in the dojo and when preparing for an exam or presentation.

5. Reflect

We often learn something new and never look back at it. Spend a few minutes reflecting on each session. Try to step outside yourself and watch how you learned or performed, then ask: how would I do this differently?

6. Develop a training ritual

Much of what we do follows a routine we carry out without thinking. Build a ritual that prepares your mind for training. The same ritual can help you prepare for a big meeting or an important day.

7. Protect your dojo time

Students who don’t make enough time for the dojo end up with gaps in their knowledge and technique. Set clear boundaries around training time, so your practice stays consistent.

8. Sit

Meditation (zazen) is not only for the dojo. You can sit anywhere. Give time to sitting and doing nothing, to reset your senses and quieten your thoughts. Mindfulness can also help to undo bad habits.

9. Smile

Smile at people every day: the best fighters are never angry. Smiling relaxes the face, which helps release tension in the body, and people enjoy being around those who smile.

10. Feel

Every movement should carry feeling and intention. You can practise this every day, whether eating or talking with someone. Do one thing at a time, and do it wholeheartedly.

11. Act with integrity

Martial artists of every style must hold themselves to the highest moral and ethical standards, in the dojo, at home and at school or work. Remember: it is much easier to get into a fight than to walk away.

I hope these rules help your training. I will end with the words of Gichin Funakoshi, the father of modern Karate:

“True Karate is this: that in daily life, one’s mind and body be trained and developed in a spirit of humility; and that in critical times, one be devoted utterly to the cause of justice.” - Gichin Funakoshi

Read more about the benefits of Shotokan Karate and five ways to become a better karateka.
